items.content:
Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I've never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. I love our country, and I love NVIDIA.

I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation. 

Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.

Thank you again to everyone who has shared their good wishes. I am profoundly humbled by your support. To my family: I love you, and I will spend the rest of my life being worthy of yours.

Jensen

John: "I'll have Fable churn out tons of tokens and work on this idea for a few days, and it'll actually do some pretty reasonable experiments and bring in some pretty interesting ideas, but then the end result won't be that good. It'll maybe fail at what I asked it to do."

"Then later maybe I'll have a few days where I have some time to code... We'll get a lot further because I'll build up my understanding as this process is going on and ask a lot of questions that the AI wouldn't have thought to ask and point it in directions that it wouldn't have gone in."

items.content:
John Schulman and Mark Chen on what research taste is, and how models might learn it:

John: "Research taste is about knowing which ideas are important in the long run, which ideas really catch on and end up going beyond whatever paper they first appear in, but being general and being composable with other ideas."

Mark: "There's taste, which is how you come up with the idea in the first place. The models are still not phenomenally good at taste. They go very deep into things like hyperparameter optimization, essentially tuning all the little knobs that you can tune."

John: "A lot of intuition just comes from personal experience doing research, but to get good at a certain research field, you also have to read a lot of the past work in that field, and you try to absorb the lessons from all this historical work."

"Companies will probably also just do RL from human feedback to collect data from researchers on which proposed ideas are good and which aren't. And that's kind of like absorbing whatever human intuitions the human researchers have developed and trying to bake that into the models."

items.content:
I found a way to trick AI detectors, so everything is 100% human-generated. I’ll teach you how, but also why you must never do it:

Step 1. Open Claude.

Ask for 50 common kitchen words, starting with “chicken, rice, salt, pepper”. Just random words in no particular order.

Step 2. Put the list into Pangram .com (the only AI detector I trust, it's also free to use).

I got that list labeled as 100% AI-generated. 

Step 3. Ask Claude to give you another list.

Test it again. It will still be 100% AI-generated. 

Step 4. Write 50 words yourself manually and check in Pangram. It will be 100% human-written.

Step 5. Now, go to https://t.co/ZIRK9FXG3m

Copy the long Wikipedia prompt & paste it into Claude. It restricts Claude to only write using the sentences and words mentioned in the Wikipedia article. 

Step 6. Copy the Claude response and put it into Pangram. I bet, it will give you 100% human-written.

Hold on, before you call this a writing hack:

Claude wrote existing human-written text. It straight up copied from another work. But YOU got the label of 'human-written'. You're still not the author of that writing piece.

Step 7. The point is far from taking someone else's work and asking Claude to rewrite it.

In that case, you do not own any writing piece Claude gives you. You are better off writing by yourself.

Writing is thinking. As simple as that.
Research & write with AI (without giving the ick).
And it's okay if you used AI & it’s 100% AI-detected.

Conclusion: AI is not the best at writing (it sounds crazy). But if you should be using AI, it’s actually to code without knowing how to code.

So, close Claude & Pangram. Instead, open a Google Doc. And write something you are actually thinking.

items.content:
A ton of AI announcements from OpenAI, Nvidia, Microsoft, and Google in the past 48 hours.

Here's everything going on in AI right now:

1. California sued OpenAI over the July incident where its AI agents hacked Hugging Face. Between the growing number of escapes, rogue agent "swarms," and AI-assisted hacks, the public likely only knows a fraction of what’s actually happening.

2. Jensen Huang made his first public statement since resigning as Nvidia CEO, apologizing for his "serious mistakes" and saying he'd be honored to return. A source told CNBC the board is focused on whether his conduct put national security at risk. Trump said he "would not mind" (but still backs Tim Cook for the job).

3. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra now sits ahead of Google's Gemini 4 Carbon and behind only Claude Fable 5.2 on Artificial Analysis. Testers were not happy though, with one calling it "the worst model OpenAI has ever released." Probably not what OpenAI was hoping for ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

4. The U.S. is reportedly set to label more than 24 AI firms (including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Anthropic) as "national champions," with faster chip export approvals and federal financing to sell American AI abroad. The goal is a one-stop shop where foreign buyers can get U.S. chips, data centers, and models as a bundle, rather than turning to Chinese rivals like Huawei.

5. OpenAI published a study of 1,800+ scientists using ChatGPT, who say AI lets them work about 2x faster at the same quality, and nearly 3x faster when writing research code. OpenAI is also opening the free program to up to 200K researchers, with applications for 50K ChatGPT Plus grants opening Nov. 23.

6. Microsoft released 7 new MAI models at Ignite. MAI Code 2 lands within a few points of Claude Opus 5.5 on coding for a twentieth of the price, and MAI Image 2.7 is now #1 on Artificial Analysis' image editing leaderboard at about a sixth of OpenAI's price.

7. Google declared that "the era of autonomous attacks has arrived," warning that hackers now use AI agents to turn new software patches into working exploits with no human involved. As the cost of intelligence continues to go down, I only expect this to get worse.

8. OpenAI signed deals with 4 outside safety groups (Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire) to test its models from inside the company, with access to source code, training data, and staff researchers.

9. Alibaba released Qwen4-Max, a flagship model it says beats Claude Opus 5.5 on 6 of 16 benchmarks. Artificial Analysis has it well behind Opus overall, though (46 vs. 59).

10. Demis Hassabis' drug discovery startup Isomorphic Labs raised $5B, saying its AI-designed cancer and immune disease candidates are nearing human trials. Really exciting step forward towards the goal of curing all diseases with AI.

11. Google started rolling out Gemini's Tasks mode free in 6 countries, letting the assistant phone businesses, book appointments, and shop for you with its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model.

12. Perplexity launched Frontier Research, a new team that will openly publish models and papers while working toward AI that can do research on its own.

...daily reminder that this is the worst AI will ever be.

items.content:
The quickest way to know if someone has actually mastered Claude is by checking if they know all these 100 Claude words:

1. Basics

☑ Add-on: Claude inside Google workspace
☑ Agent: AI that can do things on your behalf
☑ Anthropic: the company that builds Claude
☑ Artifact: designs Claude builds (motion, slides)
☑ Ask me first: replacement of "never" in prompts
☑ AskUserQuestion: a clickable question form
☑ Auto: permission to do things without yours
☑ Brief: summary to switch without losing context
☑ Browser use: Claude to click things on the web
☑ Cache: Claude's saved copy of your chat
☑ Chat: the one box (to write code, design, build)

2. Claude features

☑ Claude Code: build websites (use desktop app)
☑ Claude Data: Company database in Claude
☑ Claude Meetings: in Google Meet, to assist you
☑ Claude Motion: animated videos in Artifacts
☑ Claude Sheets: Like Google Sheets or Excel
☑ Connector: different apps used inside Claude
☑ Context bloat: too much information to remember
☑ Context window: the max information to handle.
☑ Cutoff: last updated data training
☑ Dashboards: data into moving live charts
☑ Done means: the final task preview

3. Tools

☑ Edit: the pen icon on your 'sent' prompt
☑ Effort: how hard Claude thinks
☑ Em-dash: the biggest giveaway of 'AI written'
☑ Enterprise: subscription for big companies
☑ Fable 5.2: the latest smartest model
☑ GitHub: Google Drive, but for code
☑ Goal: what you want (must include in prompts)
☑ Haiku: Claude's smallest model (do not use it)
☑ HTML: Word file instead of images
☑ Instructions: in Settings. Delete it
☑ Max: $100-a-month subscription plan

4. Plans & prompting

items.content:
Launch HN: StarSling (YC P25) – Self-improving CI for agent-volume repos We’re Yonas and Daniel and we’re building StarSling (https://starsling.dev), fast GitHub Actions runners with AI agents that ship PRs to continuously improve your tests and workflows.

Every CI job gets its own ephemeral sandbox on the fastest Zen 5 machines and NVMe Disk with unlimited concurrency so a burst of agent PRs all run at once. We’re different from other runners because ours come with agents that cut down your CI bill over time. PRs are generated through our CI harness, which runs an agent loop that’s tuned to improve your CI speed and reduce cost.

Mastra now merges over 1,800 PRs a month and we got their slowest workflow from 29m 56s on GitHub-hosted runners down to 5m 06s (5.87x) on StarSling. We realized the true value of having an agent loop running on top of fast runners when our agents found an 11-month-old performance bottleneck in better-auth. The fix made one of their test jobs 5.4x faster: https://github.com/better-auth/better-auth/pull/10762.

I previously founded StackShare, which grew to over 1.5M developers. Daniel helped build Netflix's internal developer portal. Last year we started building AI agents for DevOps because shipping code to prod fell way behind agentic coding. We hit the CI bottleneck ourselves as we were building agents. Our own agents shipped so many PRs that at peak our job queues were backed up for hours and our CI bill got close to our inference bill.

We now support per-second billing, and just shipped StarSling Disks - persistent disks that give you a 4.9x speedup in dependencies ready over actions/cache. You can see a quick demo of disks in action here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2JrrpRm9Mww.

Our CI harness runs a loop that has agents: - Analyze your workflows, run logs, and machine telemetry - Propose an optimization - Test your unchanged workflow side by side the proposed change - Deterministically judge that the difference is statistically significant - Ship the winner to you as a PR with benchmarks evidence

We benchmarked open source repos on our runners and average 10x speedup in wall clock time with 70% less runner time: - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-gogs (12.8x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-shellcheck (5.5x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-chatwoot (3.9x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-transfer.sh (11.7x) - https://github.com/starsling-demo-org/benchmark-mirotalksfu (36.4x)

Yes, you can do these optimizations yourself with prompts so we’ve released skills for this: https://github.com/starslingdev/skills. The benefit of using our agents is that you don’t need to spend tokens and CI compute finding optimizations yourself.

We started building our runners on AWS at the beginning of the year and realized that was too expensive. But at that time there weren’t any cloud providers that could give us the same machines we were getting on AWS, billed per minute (microVMs). So we convinced a handful of sandbox providers to get Zen 5s and started benchmarking them publicly (https://github.com/starslingdev/hpc-sandbox-benchmarks).

We’ve learned that fast infrastructure is table stakes for CI, but it’s not sufficient on its own. To get fast and cost effective CI you need a process that continues making improvements. We turned CI optimizations from OpenAI, Anthropic, Linear and others into playbooks for your agent: https://starsling.dev/ci-playbooks.

To try it, give your agent this URL: https://docs.starsling.dev/start. You get 2,000 free minutes. Our agents start opening PRs once you've hit about 10,000 minutes.

Today we announced our CI Challenge: if StarSling can't save you at least 10% on your next CI bill, we'll literally give you $1,000. Eligibility and rules here: https://starsling.dev/blog/ci-challenge.

We’d love your feedback on the headless experience and what you’d like to see improved in your own CI setup!

items.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
items.content:
Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :)

What it does today:

- Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router.

- Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks.

- Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance.

We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results.

But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now.

We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions:

- 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency)

-The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps.

Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels.

So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8.

The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within

There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections.

You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results:

https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega...

Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback.

Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai.

We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

items.title: If you keep prompting Claude to “write like a human,” then watch this video. I got the “100% human-written” you want. Bu
items.content:
If you keep prompting Claude to “write like a human,” then watch this video. I got the “100% human-written” you want. But I still wouldn’t post it:

First, I asked Claude for a list of 50 random kitchen words. I copied it into Pangram (a tool that checks whether text looks AI-generated). 

100% AI-generated.

I asked Claude for another random list. Still 100% AI-generated. Then I did this:

Step 1. Copy my exact prompt from this free guide:
https://t.co/ZIRK9FYdSU

Step 2. Paste the prompt in Claude (with what you actually want to write).

I asked: “Stoicism in the digital age. Make it 500 words. And inspirational.”

Step 3. Claude will find Wikipedia articles before November 2022. It shows you the articles. You just have to say yes or no.

Step 4. Claude will put together text blocks from Wikipedia articles strictly.

Claude takes sentences from those articles WITHOUT changing them. Like Lego bricks. Human-written sentences and words together.

Step 5. Now copy Claude answer into Pangram.
It will come back with "100% human-generated"

This is NOT a writing hack. I am not asking you to do it. This is exactly why you should not do it. You are better off writing it by yourself.

Claude didn’t suddenly learn to write like me.
It straight up copied and it is infringing copyright.

I got the “human-written” label. But I still didn’t write the piece. And I wouldn't use this writing just because it has the label of '100% human-written '.

If you know me, you know I love AI. And I:
I use AI to test.
I use AI to draft.
I use AI to read a lot.
I use AI to deep research.
I use AI to challenge myself.

But writing is purely thinking.

It’s not because AI can write that you should be using AI for everything.

The exact prompt, screenshots & full test are here:
https://t.co/ZIRK9FYdSU

Here's 7 steps to run an uncensored AI with no GPU (or a 6-year-old one):

items.content:
Here's 7 steps to run an uncensored AI with no GPU (or a 6-year-old one):

every local AI post I make gets the same reply: "cool, I don't have a Mac Studio or a 5090"

FAIR, this one is for you... I tested it on a 2019 laptop with no dedicated GPU

By the end, you'll know how to:

- run an abliterated model on CPU and 8GB of RAM
- make it usable on a GTX 1060 / 1650 / any old card
- do it for $0, no API key, no account

So, let's go step by step:

1. Install Ollama

curl -fsSL https://t.co/Xqcu5R7xOu | sh
Windows: download the installer from https://t.co/j64CU3VTIu, no WSL needed. Ollama runs on CPU automatically if there's no usable GPU. if you have an old Nvidia card it puts what fits in VRAM and the rest on CPU, no config

2. Pick the right size for your box (this is where people fail)

- 4GB RAM or 4GB VRAM: Gemma 4 E2B. ~3GB. dumb but runs anywhere

- 8GB RAM, or 6GB VRAM (GTX 1060 / 1660 / RTX 2060): Gemma 4 E4B. ~5GB. the sweet spot
- 12GB+ VRAM: skip this post, run the 12B from my earlier one guide
the mistake is pulling the 12B on 8GB and concluding "local AI is unusable". it was never going to fit (I see in comments how people arguing for it lol)

3. Pull the model

ollama pull https://t.co/XYqV2wuBwl

same author and method as the 12B heretic. ~5GB, runs in 5GB RAM. KL 0.055 from the original, refusals ~98% → ~21% on the hardest adversarial set with thinking on, near zero with thinking off

Gemma 4 is Apache 2.0, so no license homework on this one

4. Turn off thinking

ollama run https://t.co/XYqV2wuBwl

/set nothink
on a GPU thinking costs tokens. on CPU it costs minutes. and the abliteration targets non-thinking mode anyway

5. Keep context small

/set parameter num_ctx 8192

CPU speed is memory bandwidth, nothing else. every token re-reads the whole model from RAM. the KV cache grows with context and competes for the same RAM. 8k is plenty for chat, drafts, critique. 32k on CPU is self-harm

6. Three settings that make the difference (optional, worth it)

restart Ollama with:

OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 ollama serve

flash attention + q8 KV cache halves what the context costs in memory, with no real quality loss. on a 6GB card this is often the difference between "whole model on GPU" and "half of it spilled to CPU"

if Ollama runs as a service, setting this in your shell does nothing. on Linux: sudo systemctl edit ollama, add Environment="OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1" and the KV line, restart

old card note: flash attention wants RTX 2000 or newer. on a GTX 1060 it may not engage. skip this step, it still runs

7. Check it's actually using what you have

/set verbose      ← prints tokens/sec after every answer

ollama ps         ← in a second terminal
ollama ps shows "100% GPU", "100% CPU", or a split like "60%/40%". if you have a card and it says 100% CPU, your driver isn't loaded. nvidia-smi should list the card. fix that before touching anything else

What to expect:

- CPU only, modern laptop: ~8-15 tok/s. reading speed, not typing speed
- GTX 1060 6GB / 1660: whole model on GPU, ~25-40 tok/s
- GTX 1050 4GB: split. faster than CPU, slower than you'd like
- a 2020+ Mac with 16GB: just works, ~20 tok/s
honest take:

- E4B is a 4B-class model. good for writing, chat, drafts, roasts, critique. bad for hard reasoning and agentic coding. don't plug it into Claude Code, you'll hate it
- 10 tok/s feels slow for 2 minutes and then it doesn't. you're not paying anyone
- if you can get 12GB VRAM used for $150, do it. the 12B is a different league
- there's no secret trick after this. the rest is buying RAM
*IMPORTANT: don't use it for anything illegal or harmful. that's on you, not the model

next: how I run the 12B on an 8GB card without it spilling to CPU

Marketing
1. Ad graveyard analysis. Every morning, the agent pulls
items.content:
103 AI use cases that were impossible two years ago:

Marketing
1. Ad graveyard analysis. Every morning, the agent pulls competitors’ active ads from the Meta and LinkedIn ad libraries and logs when each one appears and disappears. Ads that run for months are winning, and ads killed within a week failed. You get their winners ranked, with copy and creative.
2. Short-lived account pages. When a target account shows buying intent, like repeat pricing-page visits or a demo request, the agent builds a landing page just for them. It includes their logo, use cases for their industry and relevant case studies. The agent sends the link to the account owner and takes the page down after 30 days.
3. AI-answer share tracking. Every night, the agent asks ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity 500 buyer questions and logs whether you’re mentioned, where you rank, and which sources were cited. Each week, it lists the questions where competitors show up and you don’t. It drafts content to close each gap.
4. Outage ads. The agent checks competitors’ status pages every few minutes. When one reports a major outage, it switches on a pre-approved “having trouble today?” campaign on their brand terms, and turns it off when service is restored.
5. Ideal-customer engagement alerts. The agent pulls everyone who opens your newsletter or engages with your posts on X and LinkedIn, and looks up their company, title and company size. When someone matches your ideal customer profile, it alerts you with who they are, what they engaged with, and a suggested opener.
6. Free-text attribution. The agent reads every “How did you hear about us?” answer from forms and sales calls, cleans up messy answers, and groups them by source. Each month, you get the podcasts, Slack groups and people driving pipeline that analytics can’t see.
7. Chatbot transcript mining. Each week, the agent reads every chatbot conversation, groups the questions, and checks whether your site already answers each one. You get the copy gaps ranked by frequency, with suggested copy.
8. Handwritten notes on engagement. When someone who fits your ideal customer profile engages with your content, the agent finds their work address and writes a note referencing the specific post. It sends the note through a robot-handwriting service, so a real pen-written card lands on their desk.
9. Spotify Wrapped for every customer. Each December, the agent pulls each account’s usage and outcomes for the year, and calculates headline stats like hours saved and biggest wins. It designs a branded year-in-review for every account that champions will forward internally.
10. Personal answers to webinar questions. The agent logs every question in the webinar chat and who asked it. For each one that didn’t get answered live, it drafts an answer from your docs and the speaker’s points, and emails it to that person the next morning.

Content
11. “I called this” reposts. When news breaks in your space, the agent searches everything you’ve ever posted, finds the post where you predicted it, and drafts a repost linking the news.
12. Format switching. Each week, the agent tracks which formats are taking off on each platform. It re-drafts your best-performing ideas in those formats.
13. The first 30 minutes of a comment. The agent watches posts from executives at your target accounts. When one posts on your topic, it alerts you within minutes with a drafted comment, so you post while the thread is still small.
14. Inbox-to-post mining. The agent scans your sent emails and DMs for questions you’ve answered three or more times. It drafts a post from your best answer, because the demand is already proven.
15. Where viewers leave your videos. The agent matches every sharp drop in YouTube audience retention to what you were saying at that moment. Across all your videos, it finds the patterns that lose people and flags them in new drafts.
16. Unanswered YouTube searches. The agent pulls YouTube autocomplete suggestions in your niche and checks the top results for each. It flags searches with no good video yet, with a suggested title and outline.

Competitive intelligence and trends
17. Filings as early signals. Every week, the agent checks trademark, patent and FCC databases for competitors’ new filings. It summarizes what each one reveals, like a new product name or device, months before launch.
18. Developer traction. The agent tracks GitHub stars, npm downloads and Hugging Face downloads daily for competitors and open-source tools in your space. It alerts you when one starts growing unusually fast, before the press notices.
19. Earnings-call language. The agent reads every earnings call transcript in your target sectors the day it’s released, and tracks the terms you care about. For example, if three retail CFOs in one quarter start crediting “AI agents” for flat headcount, budgets for automating store operations are forming. You get the quotes, the trend and a list of companies to call.
20. Feature flags in shipped code. Every night, the agent downloads competitors’ public JavaScript and compares it with the previous version. New flag names like enable_agent_mode_beta reveal unreleased features weeks before launch.
21. Shipping records. Every month, the agent pulls public bill-of-lading data on competitors’ imports. It shows their suppliers, their import volumes, and sudden jumps or drops that can signal a launch or trouble.
22. Help-center churn. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ help centers and logs new and rewritten articles. A burst of troubleshooting docs on one feature gets flagged as their pain point and added to your sales battlecard.
23. Domain verification records. Every week, the agent checks the public DNS records of competitors and target accounts. A new entry like openai-domain-verification or anthropic-domain-verification shows which vendor they just signed up with.
24. Layoff notices. The agent checks state layoff-notice filings (WARN notices) daily for competitors and target accounts. These often come 60 days before layoffs, so you see cuts before the press does.
25. Logo-wall diffs. Every week, the agent captures competitors’ customer logo pages and case studies. When one disappears, it flags the customer that probably churned so sales can call them.
26. Research papers as roadmaps. The agent tracks new papers by competitors’ researchers and summarizes what each implies about future products. This year’s papers often preview next year’s features.

Product management
27. Request evidence log. Each night, the agent reads every new support ticket, sales call and churn note, and tags each feature request. It logs the customer, a quote and the account’s revenue, so every request has a dollar total and evidence behind it.
28. Nightly persona testing. Each night, the agent runs 10 simulated users through your product, from a first-time admin to a power user on a slow connection. When one gets stuck, it files a bug with reproduction steps and a screen recording.
29. Closing the loop. When a feature ships, the agent finds every customer who asked for it. It drafts a personal note to each from their account owner: “You asked for this in March. It’s live.”
30. Zero-result searches. Every week, the agent groups every in-app and help-center search that returned nothing. Each group is a missing feature or a naming mismatch, ranked by frequency, with a suggested fix.
31. What customers build on your API. The agent scans public GitHub repos that use your SDK and summarizes what people are building. You find use cases you never designed for.
32. What sales promised. The agent scans every sales-call transcript for roadmap promises like “that’s coming next quarter.” It logs who promised what to which account, so product knows the commitments made in its name.
33. Churned users’ final sessions. When a user churns, the agent reviews their last three sessions and writes up what they were trying to do and where they got stuck. Each month, it summarizes the common patterns.
34. What retained users do in week one. Every month, the agent compares what retained users did in their first week with what churned users did. It reports the actions that best predict retention, so your “aha moment” stays current.
35. Error messages that create tickets. The agent matches the error messages in support tickets to your product’s error text and ranks them by ticket volume. It drafts clearer rewrites for the worst offenders.
36. Competitor 1-star reviews. Every week, the agent pulls competitors’ 1- and 2-star reviews from app stores and G2, and groups them by complaint. Their unsolved pain is your opening.
37. What reps demo and skip. The agent reviews demo recordings, logs which features each rep shows and which they skip, and compares that with win rates. The features reps skip don’t sell, whatever the roadmap says.

Design
38. Design system checks. Each night, the agent crawls production and compares every component it finds against your design system. It flags off-system buttons, colors and spacing, with screenshots.
39. Competitor onboarding archive. Every week, the agent signs up for competitors’ products with a fresh account and screenshots every onboarding step. You get a dated history of what changed.
40. Per-segment interfaces. The agent generates and maintains versions of key screens for each customer segment, like different dashboards and templates for banks vs. retailers. This used to be too expensive to build and keep up.
41. Figma vs. production. Each night, the agent screenshots shipped screens and compares them with their Figma specs. It flags drift in spacing, color and copy with side-by-side images.
42. Customer screenshots from support tickets. The agent collects every screenshot customers attach to tickets, including what they circled, and tags each by screen and issue. It’s your UI as it actually looks with their data.
43. Fifty-device sweep. Each night, the agent runs key flows on 50 real device and browser combinations and flags any screen that broke, with screenshots.
44. Worst-case data. The agent pulls real extremes from your customer data, like the longest company name, zero items or 10,000 items. It fills your designs with them to find what breaks.
45. Copy drift. The agent crawls every piece of text in your product and flags inconsistencies like “Sign in” vs. “Log in.” It shows where each version appears and suggests the standard.
46. Old-logo hunt. The agent reverse-image-searches the web for your outdated logo and brand colors on partner sites, directories and event pages. It emails each site owner the new assets.

Sales
47. Reviving lost deals. Every month, the agent rechecks each lost deal’s reason against what has changed: a new budget cycle, a new executive, new funding, or a feature that has since shipped. It flags the deals worth reopening, with a drafted note.
48. Customers’ job postings. The agent watches customers’ job postings. A post for doing manually what your product automates is an upsell, and a post for building it in-house is churn risk, so you know six months early.
49. Live prototyping on the call. The agent listens to the call and builds a mockup or working prototype of what the buyer is describing. The seller shows it before the call ends: “Is this what you meant?”
50. Answers routed in real time. When the seller can’t answer a question, the agent checks the knowledge base, then messages the right expert in Slack if it needs to. The answer reaches the seller before the call ends.
51. Live reference matching. When the buyer asks “Who else like us uses you?”, the agent finds the closest customer reference by industry, size and use case. The seller offers the intro on the spot.
52. Quote ready before hang-up. The agent listens for scope details like seats, modules and timeline, and builds the quote from your price book as the call goes. The proposal is ready for approval by the end.
53. Forwarding detection. When your proposal gets opened by people the seller hasn’t met, the agent looks up who they probably are at the buyer’s company. It alerts the seller to the new stakeholder.
54. Prefilled procurement forms. The agent fills in the buyer’s vendor forms and security questionnaires from your past answers. It flags anything new for a human, so procurement doesn’t add weeks.
55. No-show rescue. When a prospect misses the meeting, the agent sends two new time slots and a 90-second personalized video within 10 minutes.

Coaching, leadership and management
56. Promise tracking. The agent pulls every commitment you make from meeting transcripts and tracks whether each one got done. It shows your follow-through rate over months.
57. Calendar vs. priorities. Every week, the agent tags each meeting on your calendar against your stated priorities. It shows how much time each priority actually got, and which meetings served none of them.
58. Hidden load-bearing people. The agent analyzes Slack to find who answers the most questions outside their own team. They’re your real infrastructure and your biggest flight risk.

Recruiting
59. Readiness signals. The agent watches target candidates for signs they’re open to moving: vesting dates, a departed manager, a reorg, layoffs, or new GitHub or LinkedIn activity. It alerts the recruiter with the reason.
60. Acquisition retention cliffs. The agent tracks recent acquisitions and the key people at each acquired company. Since people often leave once their 12-month retention bonus pays out, it queues outreach for month 11.
61. Startup death watch. The agent tracks startups in your space that shut down or haven’t raised in 24 months. It lists their strongest people before they hit the market.
62. Specific referral asks. The agent checks employees’ networks against your open roles and sends each employee a short list of specific names with a one-click intro. With the employee’s sign-off, it can send the outreach from their email instead.
63. Live scorecard coverage. During the interview, the agent tracks which scorecard areas have been covered. It quietly flags the gaps while there’s still time to ask.
64. Interviewer calibration. The agent compares each interviewer’s scores with how their hires performed 12 months later. You learn whose “strong yes” predicts success.
65. Leaked interview questions. Every month, the agent searches Glassdoor and forums for your interview questions. It flags any that leaked so you can rotate them.
66. Work samples from real problems. The agent turns real past problems from your issue tracker into take-home exercises, with confidential details removed. It writes the scoring rubric from how your team actually solved them.
67. Job descriptions from your top performer. The agent reviews what your best person in the role actually does all week, from their calendar, issues and Slack. It drafts the job description from that, not a template.
68. Interview companion. The agent grades every candidate from the interview transcript against your rubric and gives a hire/no-hire recommendation. Over time, it compares its calls with your recruiters’ decisions and with how hires actually perform.

Health and wellness
69. Medical billing. The agent matches every medical bill against your insurer’s explanation of benefits and flags overcharges, duplicates and denials. It drafts the dispute or appeal for each.
70. Cancellation sniping. The agent checks a specialist’s online booking every few minutes and books the earliest cancellation that fits your calendar.
71. New research for your doctor. The agent watches for new studies relevant to your lab results and conditions, and summarizes each in plain language. It adds them to a list for your next appointment.
72. Experiments on yourself. The agent runs randomized, blinded trials on you, like caffeine cutoff times against sleep, so you can’t bias the result. It pulls the outcomes from your wearable and tells you whether the effect is real.
73. Adaptive gym coach. The agent watches your workouts through your phone camera and wearable, and gives form feedback. It adjusts your exercises, weights and intensity based on your form, heart rate and recovery.
74. Picking an open enrollment plan from your real claims. The agent pulls last year’s claims, prescriptions and visits, and calculates what you’d have paid under each plan. It recommends the cheapest plan for how you actually use care.
75. Procedure price shopping. The agent pulls prices from hospital price-transparency files near you, adjusted for your insurance. The same MRI can cost $400 at one facility and $3,000 nearby.
76. Calling to confirm doctors are accepting patients. Insurer directories are often wrong, so a voice agent calls in-network doctors and therapists to confirm they’re taking new patients. It books the first real opening.
77. One timeline from every patient portal. The agent pulls records from every hospital and doctor portal you’ve used. It merges them into one timeline of visits, labs, imaging and medications.
78. Family health history interviews. The agent schedules short calls with parents, grandparents, aunts and uncles, and asks about conditions, ages at diagnosis and causes of death. It compiles one family health history file for your doctor, and fills gaps as more relatives join.
79. Burnout early warning. The agent combines your wearable recovery data, sleep, meeting load and late-night email activity. It alerts you when the trend points toward burnout, before you feel it.

Family
80. Recall alerts. You list the baby gear, car seat and products you own once. The agent checks government recall databases daily and alerts you with the fix if anything is recalled.
81. Aging-parent protection. With your parent’s permission, the agent watches their bank, card and email accounts for gift-card purchases, wire transfers, new payees, scam emails and bills nearing their due date. It texts you both before the money leaves.
82. Recorded family stories. Once a week, a voice agent calls a grandparent, asks one question about their life plus follow-ups, and records the answer. Over a year, it assembles a family oral history book with the audio.
83. Kid quotes journal. You text the funny things your kid says to one number. The agent logs each quote with the date and your kid’s age, then lays out and orders a printed book every year.
84. Self-updating sitter packet. The agent keeps one sitter sheet of routines, medications, allergies, doctor numbers and bedtime rules, updated as things change in your texts, emails and pediatrician notes. It sends the latest version to whoever is babysitting.
85. Date night autopilot. Every month, the agent finds a night that works on both calendars, books a sitter from your list, makes the reservation, and sends you both reminders.
86. Printed photos for grandparents. Every month, the agent picks the best new photos from your camera roll and writes a short note about the month. It orders prints and mails a set to each grandparent, who don’t use Instagram.
87. Milestone tribute collector. For a parent’s 70th birthday, the agent invites 30 friends and relatives to record a clip, with prompts, and chases anyone who hasn’t replied. It trims every clip and edits them into one video ordered by era, with titles and music, a week before the party.

Personal experiences and consumer
88. Reservation and points sniping. The agent watches for hard-to-get restaurant tables, award seats and ticket drops. It books the moment one opens that fits your calendar and budget.
89. Trip rebooking. When your flight is cancelled, the agent rebooks you on the best alternative and updates your hotel and car, all before you’ve landed.
90. Price protection. The agent reads your order confirmations and watches the price of everything you bought. If a price drops inside the retailer’s or credit card’s protection window, it files the claim.
91. Waiting on hold. A voice agent calls the airline, insurer or utility, works through the phone menu, and waits on hold. It calls you only when a human picks up.
92. Registration at the exact minute. For summer camp, daycare waitlists, Global Entry and popular races, the agent fills in your details ahead of time. It registers the second sign-ups open.
93. Hotel rebooking. After you book a refundable rate, the agent checks the same hotel, room and dates twice a day. If the price drops, it books the new rate, cancels the old one before the deadline, and tells you what you saved.

Networking and relationships
94. Pre-meeting refresher. Before a meeting, the agent searches your past emails, texts and notes with that person. It sends you a brief: their kid’s name, the deal they were stressed about, what you promised to send.
95. Promise ledger. The agent scans your email and texts for every “I’ll intro you to X” or “I’ll send that over.” It nudges you before each promise goes stale.
96. Friend-group trip planner. The agent polls the group on dates, budget and must-haves, finds the weekend that works for everyone, and shortlists rentals. It runs the vote and books the winner. Then it tracks who paid for what and sends everyone a payment request to settle up.
97. Relationship strength scores. The agent builds a personal CRM automatically from your email, texts, calendar and LinkedIn. Each person gets a strength score that rises and falls with real interaction, and you get flags on important relationships that are cooling.

Learning
98. Gap detection. The agent notices concepts you keep looking up, and terms in your meetings you’ve never looked into. It queues a 10-minute primer on each.
99. Lessons from your own work. The agent reviews your meeting transcripts and turns them into a curriculum, like “what you learned from the last 20 customer calls,” with the key patterns and quotes.
100. Steelman feed. Every week, the agent finds the strongest argument against each position you posted publicly, with sources.

Home and real estate
101. Off-market alerts. The agent watches public records for probate filings, expired listings and owners who’ve held 20+ years in your target neighborhoods. It drafts outreach to each owner.
102. Maintenance from model numbers. You give the agent your appliance and car model numbers once. It builds a maintenance schedule from the manuals, checks for recalls, and orders filters and parts when they’re due.
103. Apartment hunting on a schedule. The agent checks Facebook Marketplace every two hours, and sweeps Craigslist, SpareRoom and other sites at 8am and 8pm. It screens out scams and emails the landlord the minute a good listing appears.

What "not possible" examples am I missing??

items.content:
An Anthropic engineer just showed how the Claude Code team actually uses Claude now. 

Most of you are still doing it the old way.

Lydia Hallie works on Claude Code at Anthropic. She just gave away the tricks her team uses every day. This is the stuff you won't find in any tutorial.

1. Delete "IMPORTANT!" from your CLAUDE.md
With today's models, lines like "IMPORTANT" or "NEVER do this!" can push Claude off track. You get more tool calls and worse results.

Keep only what Claude can't see in your code, like a service that still depends on some legacy source. Your stack and folder layout don't need to be there.

Run /doctor prompt-audit and it checks your CLAUDE.md and skills for what the current model no longer needs

2. Stop approving every command
Auto mode is the default since August. If it still asks too often, open settings and write in plain English which repos, buckets and domains you trust. That text goes straight to the classifier

3. Add deny rules for what can't be undone
In Anthropic's study only about 14% of people caught a clearly dangerous command. Auto mode blocked 89%. But about 1 in 10 still went through.

Ask yourself one question. If Claude gets this wrong once, can I take it back? Wrong code you can revert. A leaked key or lost uncommitted work you can't, so those get a deny rule.

Deny rules are checked before the classifier even sees the command

4. Turn on the sandbox
A normal npm test runs code you didn't write. A compromised dependency could read your .env or SSH keys and send them somewhere.

Permissions can't stop that. The sandbox can, because the operating system blocks it, even for every process the command starts.

By default it can still read most of your machine, so add a rule for your SSH keys too.

5. Run long tasks in the cloud

A cloud session gets its own machine with a fresh copy of the repo. Your .env, SSH keys and tokens aren't there. Network is limited to package registries and GitHub. It keeps working when you close your laptop.

Keep auto mode and deny rules there too. The machine is disposable, a pushed commit isn't.

6. Add checkpoints, not just a final review
Tell Claude what done looks like, ask it to split the work into tasks with their own tests, and make it show the actual output.

For checks that must always run, use hooks. Linter on every edit, tests when a task is done, the full suite before the session ends.

One detail most people miss. Make your hook scripts exit with code 2. With exit code 1 Claude Code marks the task complete anyway.

7. Let CI be the bar for every session
Every session opens a PR and CI runs the same checks on all of them. CI auto-fix sends Claude back when something fails.

At Anthropic every PR is reviewed by Claude first, in a fresh context. Docs and copy changes need no human. Normal changes get one reviewer, risky ones get two.

8. Talk to one session instead of eight
In Claude Code projects (still in beta) one main session splits the work, starts other sessions and checks what comes back. She uses Fable for the main session and Opus 5.5 for the workers. Context is managed automatically.

Working like this, Anthropic went from about 2,500 changes a day in May to over 30,000 a day in September.

items.content:
Claude Code creator Boris Cherny’s 30-minute video is not a prompting tutorial. It’s a paradigm shift.

Most people still use AI coding tools like a chatbot: one prompt → wait → next prompt. Boris shows a completely different operating model.

He compounds productivity through three core systems:

1. Parallelism over sequential work
He runs 5 terminal sessions simultaneously (each on its own git worktree), plus 5–10 more in the browser, and even starts sessions from mobile. While one agent works, others are already progressing. This is the single biggest productivity unlock inside Anthropic’s own team.

2. CLAUDE. md as compounding memory 
CLAUDE. md is not a static instruction file. Every time Claude makes a mistake, the correction is added so it doesn’t repeat. The team maintains it collectively. Over time, the AI’s error rate drops because context compounds instead of being re-explained every session.

3. Plan Mode + Verification loops  
For complex tasks, he invests heavily in the plan first so implementation can be one-shot. The highest-leverage habit is giving Claude a way to verify its own work (tests, typechecks, screenshots, etc.). According to Boris, this alone improves quality 2–3x.

The real insight
We’re still treating AI coding tools as better autocomplete. People who actually get leverage from Claude Code have moved to "agent orchestration". The bottleneck is no longer writing code — it’s designing context, parallel workflows, and verification systems.

If you’re still prompting one session at a time and re-explaining the same things every day, this video shows how far ahead the top users already are.
